blocks.x: This worksheet does one job: it stops you from changing the wrong thing first. Most businesses start with whatever is easiest to change. The workflows worth changing are the ones that happen constantly, cost real time, and carry low risk if a person reviews the output.
A spreadsheet version with automatic scoring is included in this folder: Operations-Workflow-Scoring-Worksheet.xlsx. Use whichever you prefer — the scoring is identical.
Score each workflow from 1 to 5 on three dimensions, then calculate the priority.

head: Dimension
rows: An hour or more each time

blocks.x: Risk is weighted double on purpose. A high-frequency, high-time-cost workflow that touches code or safety is not a good first candidate no matter how appealing the arithmetic looks — it is a workflow that needs a human decision, not a faster draft.
Anything scoring 5 on risk stays with a qualified person. Do not automate it because the priority score came out high. The score is an input to your judgement, not a substitute for it.
These are the workflows that exist in essentially every home-service business. Score each one honestly — the temptation is to score the annoying ones high rather than the expensive ones.

blocks.x: For each workflow, write the name of the only person who can currently perform it. If a name appears more than twice, that is your real operational risk, and the SOP Builder in folder 04 is where you should spend your effort before anything else.
What to do with the result

x: Take your top two workflows into the Prompt Library and find the section covering them.
Use those prompts for two full weeks before adding a third workflow.
Record what happens in the Weekly Operations Review.
Do not start a third workflow until the first two are habitual. Partial adoption across six workflows is worse than complete adoption across two.
